7dfcd1cde264563097ae3852dc185b3b.text: **By Cariboo Gold Dance Band hosting Juno award winning saxophonist Nov. 14** The Cariboo Gold Dance Band asks you to join them on Nov. 14 for "Swing n' Sax" with internationally known and Juno award winning saxophonist Campbell Ryga. A big band in the Williams Lake might seem a bit unusual but the Cariboo Gold Dance Band (CGDB) has been playing together for over 42 years. This 14-piece band, comprised of skilled and dedicated local musicians, played its first dance in the spring of 1984 and has performed for a wide variety of occasions in the Cariboo and beyond ever since. Each year the band brings to the community a professional to work with the CGDB and then perform as a featured artist. This year the dance band will be hosting the triple Juno award recipient and internationally respected saxophone player, Campbell Ryga. Anyone who has enjoyed the music of Michael Bublé and his Grammy winning album, _Crazy Love_, would have heard Campbell’s skillful sax playing. He has also been featured on over 87 other jazz recordings, often as a leader. Most notably, Campbell Ryga is a founding member of the award-winning Hugh Fraser Quintet. British Columbia is full of international acclaimed jazz musicians and Campbell Ryga is no exception. He was born in 1961 in Edmonton but was raised in Summerland, and is the eldest son of renowned author and playwright George Ryga. When he was 18, Ryga moved to Vancouver to pursue advanced musical studies. He has since lived and worked in Vancouver, Toronto, and New York City, establishing an international reputation as both a band leader and creative jazz artist. Ryga is currently based in Kelowna, and serves as a clinician, adjudicator, arts juror and it is a natural fit for him to be the headline performer in the Cariboo Gold Dance Band’s upcoming concert on Saturday, Nov. 14. Initial reviews were positive for “Hometown Giants,” a six-episode television series about the Langley-based WHL team, with commenters praising the behind-the-scenes look at the WHL franchise, while at least one warned it might not be suitable for young viewers. It follows the 2025-26 season of the Giants, centered on the involvement of singer Michael Buble and “Property Brothers” TV show star Drew Scott as part-owners in the campaign “to restore a team that hasn’t won a championship since 2007,” to use the words of the press release announcing the series had begun airing on Oct. 16, exclusively on Amazon’s Prime Video. “With a new coach and General Manager leading the way, the series captures the bold front-office decisions, roster-shaping trades, and high-pressure moments that define a season on the edge,” the release said. Online reviews were positive, praising the show for its focus on the young players. Movieguide.org said it was “worth the watch” while advising episodes “feature frequent foul language and some mild violence when players fight on the ice. This is an engaging watch for hockey fans and newcomers to the sport, as well as teens and adults, but the youngest viewers should skip it.” Daniel Baptista on The Movie Podcast described it as a “distinctly Canadian underdog journey that reminds you what makes sports so special. Heartfelt and hopeful, Hometown Giants is the kind of story you can’t help but cheer for.” User reviews on Internet Movie Database gave it eight out 10. “The bit where they’re in the dressing room after a tough loss and you can just see how young these kids are hits you. They’re trying to be pros but also texting their moms after the game.” Another advised that “for anyone who may not be familiar with major junior hockey it’s an interesting insight into this weird hybrid of high school, college and minor pro sports

aaa97331fdbc03d89fcd483973c5c804.text: OPINION: Community forests offer a practical path forward for B.C. | Williams Lake Tribune OPINION: Community forests offer a practical path forward for B.C. Field tour participants review an area affected by a 2022 wildfire, shown in pink on the map, on a tour with the Kaslo and District Community Forest. British Columbia’s (B.C.) forest sector is at a turning point. Communities are feeling the effects of sawmill and pulp mill closures, catastrophic wildfires, changing markets, and general uncertainty about the future. British Columbians are also asking how forests can support healthy ecosystems, sustainable local economies, reconciliation, public safety, recreation, and other community priorities. We believe community forestry offers a tested and proven way forward and should be on the minds of British Columbians and on the platforms of those running for office in the provincial election. Community forests put decisions about local forests closer to the people who understand those places and live with the outcomes. Through long-term community forest agreements, a range of local organizations—including municipalities, First Nations, community organizations, and partnerships—can manage nearby forests according to local values. And the good news? The community forest model is already working across B.C. There are 62 operating community forests, each shaped by their local landscape, economy, relationships, and priorities. More than half are held directly by First Nations or operated through partnerships involving First Nations, creating opportunities for shared stewardship, economic participation, and reconciliation. Each community forest is unique, but they share the same fundamental goals, including responsible local stewardship, economic benefits that remain in the community, and sustainable management for future generations. 2688859221752a8e410030367fa39bfc.text: The BC Conservatives have announced Pavneet Singh will run in the Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding in the 2026 provincial elecion. The BC Conservative candidate for Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream said he’s disappointed in the “sleazy attacks” made by OneBC towards him. OneBC posted court documents to Facebook on Oct. 16, regarding the indictment against Pavneet Singh in 2006. The charges were that of sexual assault, sexual touching of a person under 14 and unlawful confinement. The charges were stayed in 2008. Singh addressed the 20-year-old allegations on Facebook, stating his innocence, claiming mistaken identity in the situation and added that he has no criminal record. “In 2006, I was celebrating Canada Day in a public park. An incident with which I had nothing to do with occurred, and I was mistakenly accused of being involved,” Singh wrote. “I was falsely accused, and when the Crown prosecutor realized that, the charges were stayed.” A Crown-directed stay of proceedings in B.C. criminal court lasts for one year under section 579 of the Criminal Code, during which that time the Crown can restart the prosecution if new evidence is found. If the Crown does not restart the charges within that 12-month window, the stay becomes permanent and the matter is officially over. By general policy, the BC Prosecution Service does not provide public reasons for staying charges, except in very rare cases. “In Canada, one is presumed innocent until proven guilty – not the other way around, as my political opponents would seemingly prefer,” Singh’s social media post read. “I’m confident that British Columbians will see these despicable tactics by opponents for exactly what they are.” Black Press Media has reached out to Singh for comment and the story will be updated should comment be received. Singh is running against OneBC’s Alexandra Wright, BC NDP’s Binny Boparai and BC Green Party’s Carter Mochinski.

Owen Riegling will be performing on the CPKC Holiday Train when it makes stops across the province. Sam Roberts Band will be performing on the CPKC Holiday Train when it makes stops across the province. Sam Roberts Band and Owen Riegling are this year’s performers on the CPKC Holiday Train as it makes its way across Alberta and British Columbia this December. This is the 28th year for the holiday event which sees two trains – one which travels a predominantly Canadian route and the other mostly in the U.S. – making stops in different communities to offer free concerts, and raise money and collect non-perishable food items for food banks across North America. Cars on each of the trains are lit up in brightly coloured Christmas-themed displays. The U.S. Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 19, in Montreal, and will wind south through towns across the United States, before traveling north again into Saskatchewan, where it will make its final stop. The Canadian Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 21 in Jackman, Maine, in the United States, and will make its way west, through Quebec, down to New York, back into Ontario, then Manitoba, and into Saskatchewan, and then Alberta and B.C. “We are so proud to be part of the CPKC Holiday Train once again,” said the Sam Roberts Band online, noting it has been eight years since they last performed on the Holiday Train. Or, as they put it, “last rode the rails and rocked the mountains with you all, and we are very excited to do it all over.” From Calgary to Banff in Alberta and then from Golden, all the way to the final stop in Port Coquitlam, the band will be playing 33 shows from Dec. 11 to 20. 93d0010f0d82e9270e149a45683930c3.text: The Williams Lake Mustangs wins the mid-week home game by 4-3 against the Merrit Centennials on Tuesday, Oct. 20. The Williams Lake Mustangs narrowly beat the Merritt Centennials 4-3 in a home game on Tuesday, Oct. 20. Late in the middle frame, the Centennials answered with another goal, leaving the game tied 2-2 heading into the third. Both teams scored once in the third period, sending the game into overtime 3-3. Neither team scored in overtime, sending the game to a shootout, where the Mustangs secured a 4-3 victory. Kaelen Swanson and Braden Bolt scored the Mustang’s two second period goals before Brenden Bolt tied the game midway through the third to help send it to overtime. Logan Hauk scored the lone shootout goal, while goalie Ivan Anderson stopped all three of Merritt’s shootout attempts to secure the Mustang’s victory. Anderson finished with 42 saves on 45 shots, while Sam Saskiw stopped 44 out of 47 shots for the Centennials. The win brought Mustangs Lake to 15 points, while Centennials earned a point for the shootout loss to reach 14, according to British Columbia Hockey Conference (BCHC). The Mustangs hold 7-2-1-0 record in their inaugural BCHC season which places them 2nd in the Interior Division and 8th overall across the league. The Mustangs return to home ice oct. 30 to host the Summerland Jets, followed by the Fernie Ghostriders on Oct. 31 at Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex.

8667ecc30386cf533a0116aafddb05f2.text: Enjoying the Williams Lake First Nation fifth annual pumpkin patch were siblings Sofie and Shane Berkelaar who were joined with their mom Tanya. Picking out pumpkin to take home from the Williams Lake First Nation pumpkin patch held Friday, Oct. 16 was 8-year-old Shane Berkelaar. Down at Byron Louie Memorial Park for Williams Lake First Nation's pumpkin patch on Friday, Oct. 16 were Crystal Wells with her daughter Harper. The fifth annual pumpkin patch by Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) was the biggest one yet drawing hundreds of families to celebrate the fall season with games, hotdogs and a pumpkin to take home. This was the first year the event supporting social development programming was held at Byron Louie Memorial Park located south of Williams Lake in Sugar Cane. In 2025 the pumpkin patch was held outside the Thompson Rivers University campus in Williams Lake. WLFN manager of marketing and communications Brandon Hoffman said chief and council wanted to have it closer to community while within walking distance and still attracting as many visitors as possible. The three hour event also included family photos, bouncy castle and vendors selling lemonade, bannock, ribbon skirts and more. Organizations such as Knucwentwecw Society and Denisiqi Services Society provided activities and games including spooky decorated oreos and a ring toss. Several wooden photo stand-ins were specifically made for the day by WLFN member Michaela Gilbert. Hoffman confirmed this year’s pumpkin patch was the largest one drawing over 800 people, including more than 125 WLFN members. The remaining few pumpkins at the end of the night from Sugar Cane Ranch and Save-On-Foods didn’t go to waste with WLFN ensuring they all found useful homes.

76b5c428ed48918548ff510f067c6a22.text: A woman in Grand Forks has sustained severe injuries after being attacked by a dog in her own yard. Owners of a dog in Grand Forks are being asked to surrender their pet after it reportedly attacked and severely injured a woman. According to Kim Godidek, she was in her own yard when a bully breed dog from a neighbouring property broke through its owner’s fence and pounced on her. She said she was knocked to the ground by the canine, which reportedly inflicted four gashes on her upper thigh and broke both bones in her wrist, according to a GoFundMe page set up for her. The GoFundMe, with a goal of raising $8,000, aims to help Godidek over the next eight weeks, as she is unable to work because of her injuries. Godidek was given emergency medical attention, following the attack, before undergoing surgery, during which a metal plate was attached to her arm to stabilize it. The City of Grand Forks posted on Facebook Monday, Oct. 19, that it was in contact with Godidek, the RCMP, and the dog owner and that it is determining next steps. On Tuesday, Oct. 20, the city updated its response: “The city has engaged with the dog owner involved in the recent dangerous dog incident and is seeking the voluntary surrender of the dog. This would allow a qualified professional to conduct the required behavioural assessment.” “If voluntary surrender cannot be achieved, the city will be required to apply for a warrant to seize the animal.” The City of Grand Forks does not have a breed-specific dangerous dog bylaw and relies on a breed-neutral approach under its Animal Control Bylaw No. 2116. However, a dog can be deemed vicious if it has attacked or bitten, attempted to attack or bite, or chased any person, animal or wildlife without provocation. \*keep the vicious dog a minimum distance of 100 metres away from an elementary school, middle school, high school, daycare facility or any public park in the control area. 5165f67a61e1b1a76734f41f93948791.text: As the B.C. election approaches, NDP Leader David Eby, right, has urged supporters of Green Party Leader Emily Lowan, centre, to vote for his party, so B.C. Conservative Lorne Doerkson, left, doesn't win. With five parties fielding incumbent candidates in the upcoming provincial election, anxiety about vote-splitting has taken on a whole new dimension. In recent years, the NDP worried most often about a third-party challenger, with viable left-wing candidates running for the B.C. Greens in many ridings. But after two years of turmoil within the B.C. Conservative Party, more challengers have popped up, including CentreBC, a moderate vehicle helmed by former Conservative Elenore Sturko, and OneBC, a far-right party led by former Conservative Dallas Brodie. According to recent polling averages compiled by 338Canada, Conservatives lead overall, 45 per cent to the NDP’s 42 per cent. The Green Party trails with nine per cent, and the combined OneBC and CentreBC support sits between two and seven per cent. For this average of several polls, 338 allows for a possible four per cent swing either way for the top two parties. These polls only tell part of the story. Forecasting which party will form government is difficult by polling just the overall vote, according to Royal Roads University political communications professor David Black. “We have 93 mini-elections that generate this complex outcome we call government,” he said. Mario Canseco of the polling firm Research Co. points out that none of the smaller parties are running in every riding, either, which makes provincial polling inaccurate because some supporters won’t be able to choose those parties on their ballots. 91f1d5f562f67e8c1d6bc46318bcb6ba.text: A CMHA survey of more than 2,500 British Columbians found that 88 per cent agree a stronger mental health system means people can access help in their communities before reaching crisis, while 82 per cent agree that waiting until someone is in crisis is too late. Ahead of the B.C. provincial election, new research commissioned by the Canadian Mental Health Association, BC Division (CMHA BC) demonstrates strong public support for strengthening mental health services and investing in prevention before people reach a crisis point. And CMHA Vernon says the research reflects what staff, volunteers, and community members see every day in the North Okanagan. The survey of more than 2,500 British Columbians found that 88 per cent agree a stronger mental health system means people can access help in their communities before reaching crisis, while 82 per cent agree that waiting until someone is in crisis is too late and that investments in housing, mental health care, and community supports can prevent emergencies before they happen. “This research reinforces what community organizations have been saying for years: people want a mental health system that is accessible, proactive, and focused on prevention,” said Julia Payson, executive director of CMHA Vernon and District. “When residents consistently identify mental health and substance use as one of the most significant challenges facing their communities, governments at all levels have a responsibility to invest in solutions that work. The time to act is before a crisis occurs, not after.” The research found that mental health and substance use ranks among the top community concerns for British Columbians, with 35 per cent of respondents identifying it as one of the three biggest challenges facing their community. The issue intersects with concerns around cost of living, housing affordability, homelessness, and public safety. Beloved hockey analyst John “Cheech” Garrett was remembered and celebrated during the Vancouver Canucks game Tuesday night, Oct. 20, vs. Carolina Hurricanes. Garrett, who lived in the Boundary Park area of Surrey, stopped pucks for the Canucks and other teams during his NHL days, 1979 to 1985, before moving to the broadcast booth at Rogers Arena. Last April Garrett died suddenly, saddening fans who fondly remember his hockey knowledge, sense of humour, warm personality and love of ketchup-covered food. He was 74. “Forever a Canuck,” Garrett’s career highlights were shown on the jumbotron pre-game, before anthems were sung. “John Garrett greeted every day with an optimistic smile, always had time for an autograph, a selfie, and a story to share with his thousands of fans and friends across the hockey world,” said Al Murdoch, in-arena voice of the Canucks. Earlier, Canucks players and coaches wore fun memorial T-shirts designed with a drawing of Garrett’s famous moustache and headset on the front. “Cheech” was also subject of trivia and a “hot dog drop” during the game, won 6-3 by the defending Stanley Cup champs, previously Hartford Whalers, with whom Garrett played goal in the early 1980s. Garrett, among the most familiar voices in Canadian hockey, worked for Sportsnet until his passing.

cfbbf8b337ab5cecfd0a01b3274675fd.text: Prince George RCMP have arrested a youth following multiple break-and-enter investigations at the same pub. According to a press release, the investigations began Oct. 6, after an alarm was triggered at 2:30 a.m. at a pub located in the 200-block of Cherry Avenue. Police found a door had been forced open and suspects had entered the building. Mounties said the second break-in attempt was reported two nights later, on Oct. 8. At about 1 a.m., on Oct. 15, officers patrolling the neighbourhood noticed the pub’s exterior lights activate. Upon arriving, Mounties found three youths behind the business. Two fled, while the third remained at the scene. According to the release, after reviewing the CCTV footage from the earlier incidents, investigators determined the youth who stayed behind was likely involved in the break-ins. The youth was arrested and taken to the Prince George RCMP detachment. He was later released to a guardian and is scheduled to appear in court at a future date. “This arrest is the result of an extraordinary amount of work by our officers throughout the course of this investigation,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “Cases like this highlight the dedication, perseverance, and diligence our police officers bring to their work each day to help keep the Prince George community safe.” Police are asking anyone who can identify the two youths who fled on Oct. 15, or who has information related to these investigations, to contact the Prince George RCMP non-emergency line at 250-561-3300 or submit an anonymous tip to Northern B.C. Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477).
